reading_id.description: Rafael Calvo, Professor at the Dyson School of Design Engineering, Imperial College London, presents the lecture “Responsible Engineering Design and Innovation of AI systems.” As technologies are being developed with the promise to improve people’s lives, engineers should make ethical commitments to users similar to those that health professionals make to patients. reading_id.title: Ethical Surveillance: Regulating for personal and surveillance data in COVID-19 control conditions
reading_id.description: COVID-19 has prompted the roll out of a range of control measures and technologies adopted by authorities worldwide. As witnessed over the course of the past year, these technologies have been developed with the capacity to amass and share personal data for community control and citizen safety motivations. Nonetheless, by strengthening our existing surveillance infrastructures, they have also raised serious and as yet unanswered ethical and regulatory questions. This lecture reviews the ethical challenges—discrimination, lack of transparency, neglect of individual rights, and more—which have arisen from COVID-19 technologies and the resultant mass data accumulation. We offer a deeper look into the roll out of these control policies and technologies to regulate the movement of migrant workers in Singapore as a case study of these ethical challenges and trade-offs. We then suggest three normative foundations that need to lay the groundwork for regulatory exercises to address these ethical challenges and round off our discussion with regulatory strategies and policy recommendations.

reading_id.title: The Intersection of AI and Consumer Protection
reading_id.description: The combination of big data and AI applications in digital marketing provides firms with new opportunities to reach consumers and influence their decision-making about consumer products. Firms are able to customize their pitch to consumers through targeted advertising, and vary their pricing strategies in response to granular information about consumer responses. Many consumers continue to yield personal data that fuels this process, unaware of its implications. This lecture considers the use of consumer data in advertising for goods and services, the harms that this strategy may cause to consumer welfare and to market competition, and strategies in consumer protection law that might be used to respond to these possible harms.

reading_id.title: Profiling in the Age of AI
reading_id.description:
Profiling activities are developing in all spheres of activity. Administrations wish to better track down offenders and offer more adequate public services to citizens; companies want to understand their current and future customers better, to offer new and improved products; hospitals or medical research institutes want to fight disease or use advanced technologies to achieve better care.

Today, various technologies – IOT, big data, and artificial intelligence – are applied to radically alter methods and impacts of technology-based profiling. AI systems often operate with potential bias and errors. They rely on random statistical combinations, taking into account millions of data items that make the unprecedented, efficient, and predictive profiling of individual behavior possible. This, along with the lack of complete understanding of technology and its impacts, increases not only privacy and surveillance risks to data subjects, but to society at large. As a result, there is a need to rethink and renew regulatory frameworks for profiling in a digital environment.

reading_id.title: AI Powered Disability Discrimination: How Do You Lip Read a Robot Recruiter?
reading_id.description:
Unless the unintended consequences of ‘AI powered recruitment & HR’ are urgently addressed – hundreds of millions already disadvantaged by assumptions triggered by their disability, face lifetimes of needless economic and social exclusion.

Susan Scott-Parker OBE from Business Disability International explores the unacknowledged risks to the world’s more than 1.3 billion persons with disabilities triggered by the growing use of AI powered Human Resources Technology, asking: Why is the AI industry ignoring human reality? 
 
Should AI developers have to prove their products are ‘safe’?
Why do those concerned with gender bias ignore the fact that 1 in 5 women have a disability?
What is the difference between an AI tool that discriminates against millions and a teddy bear with buttons a child might swallow?
Who needs to do what differently – the buyers? data scientists? regulators?
How can you make a difference?

reading_id.title: Will the Market Deliver? A Business Ethics Perspective to AI
reading_id.description: This module develops a business ethics perspective on AI. After exploring the concept of AI, its ethical relevance and specific properties, the presentation addresses areas where companies can utilize AI in order to address business ethics specific issues. This includes, for example, efforts to reduce absolute poverty and to implement strategies for managing the economic, social and health challenges arising in ageing societies. reading_id.title: Autonomous Vehicles, Trolleys, and the Ethics of Machine Learning
reading_id.description: In this lecture, we take up the issue of whether and how designers of autonomous vehicles should approach programming their vehicles to respond in accident scenarios. Trolley Optimists believe that consideration of so-called trolley cases can and should be used to directly inform how autonomous vehicles should behave in such scenarios. The idea is that we can consider what we should do when, say, a runaway trolley is going to hit and kill five people but can be diverted to hit and kill only one and then program an autonomous vehicle to behave similarly. Trolley Pessimists believe it is a mistake to use trolley cases in this fashion. We outline some different versions of each of these positions, articulate some challenges to views on both sides, and then explain why careful consideration of the details of AI and machine learning justify a version of trolley pessimism.

reading_id.title: Ethics in AI: A Challenging Task
reading_id.description: In the first part of this module, we cover five current specific challenges through examples: (1) discrimination (e.g., facial recognition, justice, sharing economy, language models); (2) phrenology (e.g., biometric based predictions); (3) unfair digital commerce (e.g., exposure and popularity bias); (4) stupid models (e.g., minimal adversarial AI) and (5) indiscriminate use of computing resources (e.g., large language models). These examples do have a personal bias but set the context for the second part of the module where we address four generic challenges: (1) too many principles (e.g., principles vs. techniques), (2) cultural differences (e.g., Christian vs. Muslim); (3) regulation (e.g., privacy, antitrust) and (4) our cognitive biases. We finish with a discussion on what we can do to address these challenges in the near future.
reading_id.short_description: This module highlights five challenges from real world examples of AI in action: discrimination, phrenology, unfair digital commerce, stupid models, and the indiscriminate use of computing resources.

reading_id.title: The Intersection between AI and the Climate and Biodiversity Crisis
reading_id.description: There is no doubt that we are currently facing an urgent climate and biodiversity crisis. We need the action of all sectors and disciplines, and the best tools we have developed as humanity to accelerate change before it’s too late. AI-based technologies are among the most transformative tools that exist today. The question is, how can they best be harnessed to help fight climate change and accelerate biodiversity conservation? reading_id.title: AI Ethics: Autonomous Driving
reading_id.description: The development and implementation of autonomous vehicles is rising fast, while the scrutiny of some ethical issues fall behind. Therefore, this course module gives an overview of key ethical considerations relating to autonomous driving. In particular, the course will elaborate on the Trolley Problem, a thought experiment that has dominated the scientific debate in the field of autonomous driving ethics in the past. It will be highlighted why a move away from this concept and towards the ethics of risks is necessary and will introduce a first approach of doing so. Furthermore, the course will summarize some ethical recommendations that were developed by expert groups for industry and policymakers in the automotive sector. Lastly, the course will sketch the current status of legal frameworks.
reading_id.short_description: In this module, Professor Lütge provides an overview of key ethical considerations relating to autonomous driving. He discusses the Trolley Problem, the ethics of risk and ethical recommendations from the automotive industry.

reading_id.title: Discrimination in an Automated Society: Contributions from Latin America
reading_id.description: Do current Latin American laws protect people against discrimination due to the use of automated decision-making by artificial intelligence? How should an effective legal framework on this matter be configured? Based on these questions, this lecture analyzes this type of discrimination from the technical and regulatory point of view, provides a conceptual theory on the particularities of algorithmic discrimination situated and contextualized in Latin America, proposes the adoption of a relational principle based on a philosophical perspective, present in all Latin American indigenous peoples, and offer a new interpretive approach to the principle of equality and the concept of discrimination under a collective view, in order to overcome normative challenges evidenced in comparative law.
reading_id.short_description: Do current Latin American laws protect people against discrimination due to the use of automated decision-making by AI? This module unpacks this question and considers legal frameworks to mitigate this challenge in the context of automated societies in Latin America.

reading_id.description: This module unpacks the evolution of artificial intelligence and how it relates to human intelligence. reading_id.title: An Ethics Model for Innovation: The PiE Model
reading_id.description: How should organizations put AI ethics and responsible AI into practice? Is the answer AI ethics principles and AI ethics boards or should everyone developing AI systems become experts in ethics? In this module, Canca presents the model developed and employed at AI Ethics Lab: The Puzzle-solving in Ethics (PiE) Model. The PiE Model is a comprehensive and structured practice framework for organizations to integrate ethics into their operations as they develop and deploy AI systems. The PiE Model aims to make ethics a robust and integral part of innovation and enhance innovation through ethical puzzle-solving.

reading_id.title: Data Science against COVID-19: The Valencian Experience
reading_id.description: In this module, we explore the ELLIS Alicante Foundation’s Data-Science for COVID-19 team’s work in the Valencian region of Spain. The team was founded in response to the pandemic in March 2020 to assist policymakers in making informed, evidence-based decisions. The team tackles four different work areas: modeling human mobility, building computational epidemiological models, predictive models on the prevalence of the disease, and operating one of the largest online citizen surveys related to COVID-19 in the world. This lecture explains the four work streams and shares lessons learned from their work at the intersection between data, AI, and the pandemic.

reading_id.title: What can religion contribute to the AI debate?
reading_id.description: In this module, Bor considers the relationship between religion and AI, and religion’s possible contribution to the ethical AI debate. Using Judaism as a test case, Bor points to 7 core values that encapsulate key aspects of humanity. These values are: (1) Sanctity of the individual; (2) Virtue as foundation for knowledge; (3) Oneness and individuality; (4) Possibility of transformation; (5) Power of emotion; (6) Embodiment; and (7) Sacred time and space. By applying these values to questions around different innovations, Bor makes the case that religion can offer critical insights into how we develop and employ AI technologies in an ethical and responsible manner.

reading_id.description: In this module, Maxime Ducret and Carl Mörch discuss the ethical implications of the use of AI technologies in the field of dentistry. reading_id.title: Ethics in AI for Peace
reading_id.description: With rapid developments of data science, the greater availability of data and increased computer processing power, algorithms have become part of many spheres of our lives and work, including in peacebuilding and conflict prevention work. The “algo age” brought with it many technical, legal, and ethical questions that exceeded the scope of existing peacebuilding and peacetech ethics frameworks. This module raises awareness about these risks, and advises on how to apply tools to mitigate them by transferring ethical principles into practice to ensure that “AI ethics by design” is a first step and not an afterthought in AI for peace projects’ development and implementation.
reading_id.short_description: How is AI being leveraged in the peacetech ecosystem? How can its applications be better aligned to ethical AI principles?

reading_id.title: Ethics Applied to AI: A Matter of Cultures and Words
reading_id.description: ‘AI ethics’ has become a highly debated topic. Yet, looking closely, it appears that despite the quantity of discussions on the subject, their quality remains poor. The narrative surrounding ‘AI ethics’ (we prefer ethics applied to AI - EA2AI) is henceforth repeated without questioning its relevance and its applicability across diverse cultural contexts. This lack of critical thinking has inevitably opened the door to norms entrepreneurs, mostly from the Global North, are shaping to promote and protect their own interests, introducing a cultural bias in the debate. This lecture aims to offer some critical insights to dive deeper into the intricacies of EA2AI and to stress the need for both awareness towards the ‘AI ethics’ narrative and serious consideration for cultural perspectives.
